problem_plain: Modern AI models do enormous amounts of multiplication, but most of the numbers they multiply together are zero or nearly zero and contribute almost nothing to the final answer. Doing that arithmetic anyway wastes energy and time. In a model made of specialists — where only a few specialist sub-networks handle each piece of text — the waste is even worse: at any moment, the vast majority of the model's stored numbers are sitting idle. The challenge is figuring out which work can be safely skipped, communicating that decision to the hardware fast enough, and actually avoiding the load-and-compute cycle for the parts that do not matter.
why_plain: Bandwidth — how fast data moves — is the real constraint: pulling a number out of memory chips costs far more energy than doing arithmetic on it once it arrives. So the biggest win comes from never loading the useless zeros at all, not merely from skipping the multiply once a number is already on-chip.
approach_plain: The papers in this theme all exploit the same observation: at any moment, only a small fraction of a model's stored numbers are non-zero and worth computing with. They find that active fraction — sometimes at the level of individual bits, sometimes at the level of whole specialist sub-networks — and then redesign how data is laid out, how hardware is wired, or how work is scheduled so that the zero-valued or idle portions are never fetched, never routed, and never multiplied. Some papers remove useless numbers before the model is ever deployed; others decide what to skip on the fly while the model is answering a question; others reorganize where data lives so the active slice can be read in one fast burst rather than many scattered trips.

groups.heading: Models made of specialists: routing traffic and hiding communication delays
groups.explain: In a model made of specialists, the network contains many independent sub-networks. Each piece of input text is sent to only two or three of them. This means the vast majority of the model's stored numbers sit idle for any given input — exactly the skipping-unimportant-numbers opportunity we want. The engineering challenge is that routing decisions must be sent across machines, the right stored numbers must be fetched at the right moment, and the delay caused by chips talking to each other can dominate total time if not carefully hidden behind useful work.

papers.name: MoC-System
papers.gloss: Saves only the specialist sub-networks that actually ran during each training step when writing crash-recovery snapshots, shrinking snapshot size dramatically.

papers.name: MoE-Lightning
papers.gloss: Streams specialist weights from main memory to the GPU in pages, overlapping the data transfer with computation of the previous specialist; achieves 10.3x higher output rate than earlier offloading approaches on a single small GPU.

papers.name: Klotski
papers.gloss: Keeps several questions in flight at once so that inputs from different questions that need the same specialist are grouped together, making each specialist's computation long enough to hide the time spent loading it.

papers.name: FSMoE
papers.gloss: Overlaps both within-machine and between-machine messages with specialist computation using a three-stage pipeline whose chunk sizes are tuned per workload by a simple performance formula; 1.19x to 3.01x faster than a leading prior approach on real models.

papers.name: COMET
papers.gloss: Merges the step of sending inputs between chips and the step of doing the multiplication into one continuous operation, so computation on locally available inputs starts immediately without waiting for all messages to arrive; hides 86.5% of communication time, giving 1.71x end-to-end speedup.

groups.heading: Deciding at runtime which neurons to skip
groups.explain: Many layers inside a model produce output values where most are zero or very small after a shaping step is applied. If you can predict which values will be negligible before doing the full computation, you can skip loading the corresponding stored numbers entirely. The trick is that this prediction must be cheap — the cost of deciding what to skip must be less than the work saved.

papers.name: Neuralink
papers.gloss: Reorganizes which neurons are stored next to each other in a phone's flash memory so that neurons that tend to fire together are physically adjacent, turning scattered random reads into fast sequential reads; 1.49x average speed improvement on the device.

papers.name: DIP / DIP-CA
papers.gloss: Picks only the largest-valued inputs to each layer at runtime and skips the corresponding stored-number columns entirely; a memory-aware variant biases selection toward columns already in fast on-chip memory, cutting memory-chip traffic by 46% and raising output rate 40%.

papers.name: EXION
papers.gloss: Exploits two kinds of skippable work in image-generation models: across hundreds of image-refinement steps most intermediate results repeat (70–97% of one key layer's outputs are reused rather than recomputed), and within each step most attention scores are negligible; a custom chip achieves 3.2–379x speedup over a server GPU with barely noticeable quality loss.

groups.heading: Skipping zeros in regular patterns the hardware can exploit efficiently
groups.explain: Removing individual random zeros from a table of stored weights is hard to exploit in hardware because the remaining non-zero values end up at irregular locations. If instead zeros are forced into a regular pattern — for example, exactly two zeros in every group of four weights — the hardware can use a fixed-size compact format with no extra bookkeeping. The trade-off is that a more regular pattern is easier for hardware but strays further from the ideal arrangement, which can hurt accuracy.

papers.name: TB-STC
papers.gloss: Finds a two-dimensional block zero-pattern that works for both the forward pass and the backward pass through the same weight table, exploiting their mathematical mirror relationship; improves energy times delay by 3.82x and recovers up to 2.58% of the accuracy lost by simpler zero-pattern methods.

papers.name: xDecimate / MATCH
papers.gloss: Adds a single new instruction to a small processor that selects and multiplies only the non-zero entries from a semi-regular zero-pattern in one hardware step; achieves 3.21x speedup on an image classifier at just 5% extra chip area.

papers.name: TASD / TTC
papers.gloss: Breaks any irregularly zero-scattered weight table into a sum of regularly patterned pieces using basic arithmetic properties, so a chip designed only for regular zero-patterns can run any model without retraining; 39% speedup on hardware that natively supports regular zero-patterns with 99% of model quality preserved.

papers.name: BADA
papers.gloss: Skips computation at the level of individual groups of bits within a number — whenever either the weight or the input bit-group is all zeros — combined with training tricks that push more bits toward zero; 2.67x higher output rate and 2.15x better energy efficiency over the prior best bit-level design.

papers.name: CROSS
papers.gloss: A compiler that routes each piece of a model's computation to whichever of a zero-skipping path or a fast all-numbers path finishes faster, using a translation step to make the zero-skipping work compatible with highly optimized dense math routines; 2.03x average speedup over seven competing methods.

groups.heading: On-off pulse networks: skipping work when signals are silent
groups.explain: Some AI networks are inspired by biology and communicate using discrete on/off pulses rather than continuous numbers. Because a zero pulse means the neuron is silent, a network where most neurons are quiet at any moment means most multiplications can be replaced by simple additions or skipped entirely. This extreme skipping makes these networks very energy-efficient — if the hardware and training are designed to exploit the silence.

papers.name: Prosperity
papers.gloss: Notices that two rows of a weight table multiplied by identical on/off pulse patterns give identical results; computes each unique pattern's result once and reuses it for all matching rows; 7.4x faster and 8x more energy-efficient than a prior pulse-network chip.

papers.name: Phi
papers.gloss: Groups common pulse patterns before deployment, pre-computes their products with the weights, and at runtime uses a lookup table to retrieve results instead of multiplying; a small correction step handles the remainder; 3.45x faster and 4.93x more energy-efficient than prior pulse-network chips.

papers.name: Bishop
papers.gloss: Packs pulse data across both inputs and time steps into bundles, sends high-density bundles to fast multiply hardware and low-density bundles to efficient skip-zero hardware, replacing most multiplications with simpler AND-and-add operations on binary pulses; 5.91x speedup and over 6x energy improvement.

papers.name: Bio-FO
papers.gloss: Trains each layer of a network using only forward passes and a fixed random projection, eliminating the need to store all the intermediate values needed by the standard backward-pass training method; up to 19.8x energy reduction and 3x memory reduction versus prior forward-only training on an edge device.

groups.heading: Skipping zeros in graphs and scientific data
groups.explain: Many tasks outside of AI — analyzing social networks, matching text patterns, running physics simulations — naturally produce data tables where most entries are zero because most pairs of items are not connected. Multiplying or solving equations with these mostly-zero tables using hardware designed for fully-filled tables wastes enormous bandwidth fetching zeros. The solutions here redesign data layout, reorder access patterns, or repurpose existing hardware to handle the irregular structure of mostly-zero data.

papers.name: Hopps
papers.gloss: Tracks only the pattern-matching machines that are currently active for each input character using a compressed yes/no map, skipping all idle ones; stores the active machines' next-step tables in side-by-side memory locations to reduce trips to memory chips.

papers.name: SparseWeaver
papers.gloss: Adds a small hardware unit to GPU cores that converts irregular graph operations into balanced fully-filled operations on the fly, using the graph's own connection structure to avoid stalls where one core waits for another; 2.36x faster than prior balancing schemes.

papers.name: SPASM
papers.gloss: Builds a library of common data-access-pattern templates for mostly-zero table-times-column-vector multiplication and picks among them at runtime per tile; 2.81x speedup over a fixed-pattern chip without sacrificing the ability to handle new patterns.

papers.name: HSMU-SpGEMM
papers.gloss: Redesigns the running-total accumulator for multiplying two mostly-zero tables so more active data fits into fast on-chip memory at once while collisions — two results needing the same slot — happen less often; outperforms four leading GPU tools for this operation.

papers.name: AccelES
papers.gloss: Uses a low-precision compressed version of a mostly-zero table to cheaply identify the top candidates, then applies full-precision scoring only to those candidates; 3.4x faster than a programmable-chip baseline and 153x faster than a general-purpose CPU for recommendation lookups.

papers.name: Telos
papers.gloss: Speeds up the one-at-a-time bottleneck in physics equation solvers — where each answer depends on the previous one — by arranging computation across processing units in a pipeline that respects the regular zero-pattern of grid-based simulations; 61x faster than a CPU and 8x faster than a GPU.

papers.name: RT+SpMSpM
papers.gloss: Repurposes the ray-tracing collision-detection units built into modern GPUs to find which output positions in a mostly-zero table multiplication are non-zero, then adds a small totaling engine using just 0.2% extra chip area to compute those products at the same time; 3.06x faster than the leading GPU tool for this operation.

papers.name: SparseTransX
papers.gloss: Replaces the costly scatter-and-gather data shuffling in knowledge-graph training with a single mostly-zero table multiply by encoding which items appear in each training example as a compact yes/no table; 5.3x CPU and 4.2x GPU speedup with 11x memory reduction on large datasets.

papers.name: Bootes
papers.gloss: Reorders the rows of one input table before multiplying two mostly-zero tables, grouping rows with overlapping non-zero positions so they share already-fetched data; reduces trips to memory chips by 2.31x compared to a leading chip design.

papers.name: Misam
papers.gloss: Uses a lightweight decision-tree to predict the best computation strategy from structural features of the input table, then reprograms a flexible chip on the fly to use a specialized layout for that strategy; up to 10.76x speedup by switching strategies adaptively.

groups.heading: Hardware and compiler plumbing that makes skipping zeros practical
groups.explain: Even when we know which computations to skip, turning that knowledge into real speedups requires solving coordination problems: fast on-chip memory must store irregularly shaped non-zero data without wasting space, the hardware must be flexible enough to handle many different zero-patterns, and the software that translates programs into chip instructions must map zero-skipping computations efficiently. These papers build the underlying infrastructure that makes skipping unimportant numbers practical across a wide variety of tasks.

papers.name: HYTE
papers.gloss: Divides the problem of choosing how to tile a mostly-zero data table into an offline sampling pass that picks a near-optimal starting tile shape and a runtime pass that adjusts that shape as local density varies; 3.3x to 6.2x faster than fixed tiling strategies.

papers.name: FlexNeRFer
papers.gloss: A single chip that supports multiple data-movement patterns and automatically picks the best compact storage format at runtime based on how many non-zero values it observes; 8.22–43.3x faster than an equivalent GPU for generating 3D scenes from a neural model.

papers.name: Quartz
papers.gloss: A flexible chip with distributed fast on-chip memory banks whose data-flow can be reprogrammed at runtime to match the access pattern of any zero-skipping computation — whether for graphs, AI models, or math solvers; full speed numbers not reported in the abstract.

papers.name: SeaCache
papers.gloss: A fast on-chip memory store that packs variable-length rows of mostly-zero data into fixed-size slots, then dynamically splits its space between actual data and bookkeeping based on measured reuse rates; 2.8x better than prior zero-skipping memory designs.

Treats tile-size selection for mostly-zero data as a probability problem, predicting how often data will already be in fast on-chip memory from the statistical spread of non-zero positions, without needing to see the full input at compile time; detailed speed results not available from the abstract.

papers.name: Transitive Array
papers.gloss: Identifies when a partial product needed in a multiplication has already been computed earlier in the same batch and reuses it via a dependency map, enabling a chip design with no multipliers at all; 7.46x faster than a leading low-precision chip on AI model answering.

groups.heading: Trimming the model before deployment: removing whole layers or neurons
groups.explain: Rather than skipping zeros at runtime, trimming removes parts of a model permanently before it is ever used. Structured trimming removes entire layers or blocks, which is clean and efficient but can hurt accuracy. The key insight here is that the original full model is still available after trimming and can be used to generate better training examples for the smaller trimmed model, partially recovering the lost quality.

papers.gloss: Permanently removes entire processing blocks from a language model by keeping those whose outputs differ most from their inputs — blocks that just copy their input carry redundant information — then uses the untrimmed model to rewrite the fine-tuning examples so the trimmed model learns from outputs matched to its new, smaller capacity.

papers.name: MetaSapiens
papers.gloss: Cuts the number of tiny 3D scene-building pieces in a neural rendering model based on each piece's visual contribution and hardware cost, then renders the edges of the screen at lower detail since the human eye sees less sharply away from the center of gaze; claims real-time neural scene rendering on a mobile phone.

Selects a maximally varied small subset from a billion-example training dataset by spreading the selection algorithm across many machines and computing upper bounds on each example's added value without gathering all data in one place; achieves 98% of the quality of centralized selection.

connect: Every technique in this theme is ultimately a strategy for moving less data: by skipping zero weights, sending inputs only to the specialist sub-networks that need them, or reusing previously computed results, these systems reduce the number of trips to memory chips needed per answer. Since reading from memory costs far more energy than doing arithmetic, skipping the work that does not matter translates almost directly into lower energy use and faster answers — not because the math got faster, but because the chip stopped paying for data it never needed.
